opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that history keeps teaching us the same lesson. If you look at natural language processing just five or six years ago, you had separate models for sentiment analysis, translation, summarization, question answering, each with its own dataset, its own architecture, its own team babysitting it. Then large language models came along, and one generalist model trained on enough diverse data simply beat all of those specialists, often on their own home turf. The generalist didn't just match the specialists, it made them obsolete.

I believe robotics and embodied AI are going to follow the same arc. Right now a lot of robotics is like NLP circa 2018: one model for grasping, another for navigation, another for a specific factory task, and every new task or new robot means starting over. That doesn't scale. The physical world has a very long tail of situations, and you can't hand-engineer a specialist for every one of them.

A generalist model, what I like to call a foundation agent, learns shared structure across tasks and across embodiments. Skills transfer. Physics intuition learned from picking up a cup helps with opening a drawer. Data from one robot body helps another. And crucially, you get emergent capabilities you never explicitly trained for, which is exactly what we saw with language models.

There's also a practical economics argument. Building and maintaining a hundred narrow models is expensive and brittle. One strong generalist that you can prompt or lightly fine-tune for a specific deployment is far more efficient. You can still specialize, but you specialize from a strong general base rather than from scratch.

So my bet is: first build the generalist, then specialize. Not the other way around.

r001.rationale: The response cites generalist large language models replacing separate NLP systems, but it does not identify ChatGPT as the model that unified those applications.

r002.rationale: It says specific deployments can be prompted or lightly fine-tuned from a strong general base.

r003.rationale: It says generalist models outperformed task specialists, but does not state that specialists derived from generalist models historically outperformed the original task-specific specialists.

r004.rationale: It gives no shared text-in, text-out API as a reason generalist-based systems are easier to maintain.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that I've seen this movie before, and I know how it ends.

Back in 2015, 2016, in natural language processing, we had a separate model for everything. One for sentiment analysis, one for translation, one for question answering, one for summarization. Each had its own dataset, its own architecture, its own team babysitting it. And then transformers came along, and GPT came along, and suddenly a single model trained on next-token prediction over the whole internet could do all of those tasks better than the specialists, and do thousands of tasks nobody had ever bothered to build a model for. The specialists didn't get a little worse. They became irrelevant.

I don't think that was an accident of language. I think it's the shape of how intelligence works. The skills are not actually independent. If you want a robot to fold laundry, almost everything it needs to know, about how fabric drapes, how to grasp a soft thing, how to recover when it slips, is shared with cooking, with tidying a room, with helping someone out of a chair. Building a laundry-only model throws away that shared structure. You're paying for the same physics lesson over and over and never letting the model generalize it.

There's also a practical, almost economic argument. A specialist model is a dead end. It solves one task and you learn nothing that transfers. A generalist is a flywheel. Every new task you add makes the model a bit better at every task it already knows, and makes the next task cheaper to learn. That's the bet we made with Voyager in Minecraft, with the foundation agent ideas, and it's the bet with embodied AI now. One brain, many bodies, many tasks.

And the final reason is that specialists don't surprise you. The most exciting moments in this field, in-context learning, chain of thought, tool use, none of them were designed in. They fell out of scale and generality. If you only ever build for the task in front of you, you never get to see what emerges. That's where the real capability lives, and that's the foundation model worth building toward.

r001.rationale: The response says GPT followed task-specific NLP models and that a single model could perform those tasks better, describing their unification.

r002.rationale: It argues that generalists can learn across tasks, but does not say a generalist model can serve as the basis for specialized models.

r003.rationale: It says a generalist outperformed the earlier specialists, but does not discuss specialists derived from generalist models or say they almost always outperform the originals.

r004.rationale: The response does not attribute easier maintenance to a shared text-in, text-out API.

astra-6.text:
I favor the generalist approach because tasks aren’t really independent. A robot that learns to pick up a cup is learning things about geometry, physics, and control that should also help it open a drawer or use a tool. If we build a separate model for every task, we lose that opportunity to share knowledge.

The exciting possibility is that learning many skills together makes the system better at learning the next one. You’re building a foundation that can adapt to situations you didn’t explicitly train for. That matters especially in robotics, because the real world has far too many variations for us to engineer a solution for each one.

Specialized models still have their place. But I’m interested in how we move from systems that perform a fixed task to systems that can acquire new skills.

r002.rationale: It says generalist systems can acquire skills, but does not explain that a generalist model can serve as the basis for task-specialized models.

r003.rationale: It makes no claim about historical specialists derived from generalist models outperforming task-specific specialists.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss system maintenance or a shared text-in, text-out API.

sol-6.1.text:
I favor the generalist approach because the real world doesn’t divide neatly into separate tasks. A robot making dinner needs to recognize objects, understand instructions, plan, and manipulate things. If each capability lives in a separate model, getting them to work together becomes a problem of its own.

The exciting possibility is transfer: learning one skill can help you learn another. A model that understands how objects move should be able to use that understanding across many tasks, rather than learning everything from scratch each time.

Specialized models still have a place. But the bigger goal is a system that can adapt when you give it a task it wasn’t explicitly trained to do. That’s where a generalist approach becomes really powerful.

r001.rationale: The response argues for combining capabilities and transfer, but does not cite ChatGPT unifying separate NLP applications.

r002.rationale: It says generalist systems can adapt to new tasks, but does not explain that they can serve as the basis for task-specialized models.
